questions.q: The power goes off. Which one loses its data?
questions.explain: RAM and caches are volatile: they forget everything without power. Disks keep their data. That is why orders must be saved to disk.

questions.q: Put these in order, from fastest to slowest.
options: CPU cache, RAM, SSD, server in another country
questions.explain: Cache (about 1 ns) → RAM (about 100 ns) → SSD (about 0.1 ms) → another country (about 200 ms).

questions.q: Without os.fsync(), saving an order took about 900 ns instead of 335 µs. Why not always skip fsync?
options: fsync is needed for the file to have a name
Without it, the order may still be only in RAM, and a power cut would lose it
questions.explain: The OS keeps writes in RAM and saves them later. fsync forces them onto the disk now. Databases use it for every saved order.

questions.q: Your internet plan is 100 Mbps. What is the fastest you can download a file?
questions.explain: Mbps is megaBITS per second. 1 byte = 8 bits, so 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 megaBYTES per second.

questions.q: A page asks the inventory service for stock 100 times, once per product. What is a better way?
options: Ask for all 100 products in one network trip
Buy a CPU with more GHz
questions.explain: Every network trip is thousands of times slower than RAM. Fewer trips means a faster page.

questions.q: (Going deeper) The CPU repeats one loop billions of times per second. What is it?
options: Fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it
Read the disk, write the disk
Open a file, close a file
questions.explain: Every program, including Python itself, is a long list of simple instructions the CPU fetches, decodes and executes.

questions.q: (Going deeper) In the lab, reading 10 million prices in random order took about 2.4 times longer than in order. Why?
options: In order, each trip to RAM brings a whole cache line of neighbours into the cache; random reads keep missing the cache
Python can't read in random order
questions.explain: This is spatial locality. Caches work best when you read data that sits next to what you read before.

questions.q: (Going deeper) Bazaar's servers in Mumbai, customers in New York: every small request takes about 200 ms. Will a connection with more bandwidth fix it?
options: Yes, more bandwidth always means faster
No: small requests are slow because of latency (distance, the speed of light); you need fewer trips or servers closer to the customers
No, because New York has no internet
questions.explain: Bandwidth is the width of the pipe, latency its length. Light alone needs about 125 ms for that round trip.
